senses: The quality of being commensurable or commensurate
Any of several varieties of eating apple that have a yellow or green skin with patches of red.
Any of several roundish or oblate apple varieties.
An apple tree raised from a seed (not grafted) or its fruit.
ety: Probably from Middle English pipin (“a seed”), as being raised from the seed.

senses: The amount that a fork will hold.
examples: He uncovered the fragrant eggs and b., and I pronged a moody forkful.

senses: A student who graduates with second class ("senior optime") or third class ("junior optime") honours in mathematics, or (loosely) in any other subject.
ety: Borrowed from Latin optimē (“very well”), in the phrase optimē disputāstī (“you have disputed very well”), formerly used in reporting results at Cambridge.

senses: A bird of the family Cacatuidae with a curved beak and a zygodactyl foot.
ety: Borrowed from Dutch kaketoe, borrowed from Malay kakaktua. Spelling influenced by cock.
examples: We saw some cockatoos in the aviary.

senses: To hold the hair and comb it towards the head, thus giving it a bushier look.
examples: Her dark-blonde hair, worn long at Oxford, had been cut and backcombed, Diana-style, and quivered when she shook her head.

senses: Having bark.
Prone to bark, to make the sound of a dog.
Sounding like the bark of a dog.
A small or microscopic cosmos; a microcosm.
examples: So the double men of Aristophanes are microcosmoi (p. 566); as the world is divided, so are they.

senses: Misinterpretation or misunderstanding; (countable) an instance of this; a mistake.
Incorrect or unfair suspicion; (countable) an instance of this.
ety: From Late Middle English misprision, mesprision (“criminal offence or illegal action, especially one committed by a public official”) [and other forms], from Anglo-Norman misprision, mesprision, mesprison (“criminal offence or illegal action; error, mistake, specifically an error by a court”) [and other forms] (whence Late Latin mesprisio, misprisio), and Old French mesprison, from mespris (“contempt, disdain”) (modern French mépris) + -ion (suffix indicating a condition or state). Mespris is the past participle of mesprendre (“to misunderstand”), from mes- (prefix meaning ‘badly; wrongly’) +

senses: one who defends; a defender
Having great extent.
The phenomenon of the Earth revolving around the Sun.
ety: Shortened from heliocentricism, from heliocentric + -ism, from Ancient Greek ἥλῐος (hḗlĭos, “sun”) + κέντρον (kéntron, “centre”), equivalent to helio- + -centrism.
examples: Heliocentrism is not yet universally known or accepted. In a 1999 poll, 18 of Americans said that the sun revolves around the Earth, while 79 percent said Earth revolves around the sun.

senses: A scientist, usually a medical doctor, who specializes in haematology.
The coastal land bordering a sea or an ocean.
The foreshore, the strip of land between low water and high water.
The injection of a venom by means of a sting, etc.
The deterioration in the surface quality of a plastic that is in contact with another material.
examples: No one knows how well ratels can count in the ratel-bee brinkmanship game, but they likely can sense when a dangerous level of envenomation is near.
Following a letter ballot of D-20. new definitions of plasticizer, reinforced plastics, filler, A-stage, B-stage, C-stage, and envenomation, will be sent to the standards committee.

senses: papa, father (as a respectful term of address)
A professional who has earned a diploma.
ety: From diploma + -ate (suffix forming nouns denoting rank or office).
examples: You think he could barter and cheat / As vulgar diplomates use, / With the people's heart in his breast?

senses: A fictional drug obtained from human adrenal glands.
Related to bionics.
Having been enhanced by electronic, mechanical, or mechatronical parts; cyborg.
ety: Blend of bio- + electronic. The superhuman sense is attributed to the TV shows The Six Million Dollar Man (1973–1978) and The Bionic Woman (1976–1978).

senses: The act of precluding.
ety: Borrowed from Latin praeclusio, praeclusionis, from Latin praecludo.

senses: Having on a kilt.
Plaited after the manner of kilting.
Tucked or fastened up; said of petticoats, etc.
In search of employment.
Cannabis resin, used as an intoxicant in North India and Pakistan.
examples: She had not smoked the charas to abdicate responsibility but to be sure of seizing her opportunity

senses: An atom of this element.
ety: From Ancient Greek λανθάνω (lanthánō, “to escape notice”) + -um (“a chemical element”), because it had gone long undetected in mineral ores.

senses: A scientist whose speciality is agronomy.
The condition where a church's leaders have severed ties to a larger body and thus no longer report to a higher authority.
A white person (Caucasian person), especially white settler in Australia, especially a man (especially as opposed to an Aboriginal Australian).
examples: Indigenous self-representation was contained within a mainstream vision. This was clearly a whitefellas′ appropriation of blackfellas′ dreaming.

senses: One of the five canons of classical rhetoric: the discipline of memory and recall.
ety: Borrowed from Latin memoria, from memor (“mindful, remembering”). Doublet of memoir and memory.

senses: Technical terms or objects; things pertaining to the practice of an art or science.
The doctrine of arts in general; those branches of learning that relate to the arts.
ety: Partly from Latin technicus and partly from Ancient Greek τεχνικός (tekhnikós); probably modelled on German Technik. Doublet of technique.

senses: Covered with fine hair.
Tending to create an illusion.
examples: Many have illusionistic carved stone frames, which make them seem like windows to the outdoors.

senses: One who does skywriting. A pilot who writes messages, by leaving a trail of smoke from the plane, that are visible from the ground.
Having, or pertaining to, three distinct states.
examples: This tristate logic deals with true, false, and unknown values.

senses: The act of replenishing.
A new supply of something.
A type of pickled daikon radish, half-dried before being pickled with rice bran and salt or sugar, typically yellow in color.
examples: When daikon is pickled in a paste of salt and rice bran it is called takuan and in this form or in the fresh state it is utilized when available by the majority of Japanese families for every meal.
Hot rice with takuan is as common on Japanese tables as bread and butter in America.
It began to snow heavily once again whilst the two samurai slowly ate their breakfast of rice and takuan radish

senses: Of fifth rank or order.
Consisting of five things; arranged in fives.
To the base of five; represented by the numerals 0, 1, 2, 3 and 4.
ety: From the Latin quīnārius (“containing five each”), from quīnī (“five each”, “five at a time”) + -ārius (whence the English suffix -ary); compare the French quinaire, the Italian quinario, and the Portuguese quinário. Doublet of quinarius.

senses: A sour spice popular in the Eastern Mediterranean, made from the berries of tanner's sumac.
ety: The noun is derived from Middle English sumac, asimac, simak, sumak, symak (“portions of the shrub Rhus coriaria, chiefly used for medicinal purposes”), from Anglo-Norman sumak, symak, and Old French sumac, or directly from its etymon Medieval Latin sumach, sumac, from Arabic سُمَّاق (summāq), from Classical Syriac ܣܘܡܩܐ (summāqā, “red; sumac”). The English word is cognate with Italian sommaco, sommacco, Occitan simac, Portuguese sumagre, Spanish zumaque. The verb is derived from the noun.

senses: A cable TV control center, at which terrestrial and satellite signals are received, monitored and injected into the cable network.
examples: The headend cable modem handles the medium access control (MAC) protocol which is necessary for point-to-multipoint operation on the tree-and-branch network.

senses: Resembling metal music.
The process of removing materials that are absorbed with a solvent.
